Mitochondria. These are the membrane-bound organelles responsible for cellular respiration, converting nutrients like glucose and fatty acids into usable energy in the form of ATP. Present in nearly all eukaryotic cells, mitochondria have earned their nickname as the powerhouse of the cell due to their essential role in energy production. What makes them particularly interesting is that they contain their own DNA and ribosomes, reflecting their evolutionary origin as free-living bacteria.

The mitochondrial structure is carefully organized. There's an outer membrane that's relatively permeable, and an inner membrane that's highly folded into structures called cristae. These folds maximize the surface area available for the electron transport chain. The innermost compartment is the matrix, and this is where the Krebs cycle occurs.

Through aerobic respiration, mitochondria use oxygen to extract maximum energy from glucose—approximately thirty to thirty-two ATP molecules per glucose molecule. This is far more efficient than anaerobic respiration. The mitochondrial DNA encodes some respiratory proteins, and the mitochondrion maintains its own ribosomes—seventy-S ribosomes similar to prokaryotic ribosomes—which allows it to synthesize some of its own proteins. In most organisms, mitochondria are inherited maternally.

Mitochondria evolved billions of years ago through endosymbiosis, when eukaryotic cells engulfed alpha-proteobacteria. This partnership fundamentally transformed eukaryotic life by enabling efficient aerobic respiration. The ability to extract far more energy from nutrients than prokaryotic ancestors could fueled the evolution of larger, more metabolically active cells. Today, mitochondrial dysfunction underlies numerous human diseases including diabetes, Parkinson's disease, and cardiac disease, highlighting their clinical significance.
